searchText: <vbuterin> Remind me, who is working on code merklization? I think just you. 😬 (🚎) <vbuterin> Wait.... I'm pretty sure there's a proper working group on the topic and I've talked to them Also, you may have better luck in <#690694464855081060> (though, maybe that isn't bridged to wherever you are). <vbuterin> right, I guess it's that channel There's team X from PegaSys, <@!296630428754771968> as well who collected some numbers. I believe a turbo-geth team member is trying to figure out if we can get away mostly with static jumps, which if is the case would be beneficial for code merkleization. I also ran some experiments and am starting work on a draft spec. (and of course others who contributed to the conversation) <vbuterin> What do you mean by "get away with static jumps"? Like banning dynamic jumps from the EVM? no, it is proving that most (maybe 99.9% or something) deployed contracts cannot jump into an invalid jumpdest (JUMPDEST which in inside the data of a PUSHx instruction). If that proving can be done efficiently before any contract is deployed, then you can a) not do jumpdest analysis for this contract b) merkelise it any way you want <vbuterin> Ah I see but the approach we are taking is not just going to be useful for code merklelisation. It may help to potentially identify contracts that have only SSA (static state access), and I suspect most transactions are actually SSA. This can lead to some interesting optimisations related to parallelisation, without having to explicitly mark access lists we are doing what it is called "abstract interpretation" <vbuterin> Is that the same as symbolic execution? Or something different? (re @eth1x_bridge_bot: <Alexey> we are doing what it is called "abstract interpretation") It is different from symbolic execution, because in symbolic execution you are still trying to follow the execution path of some sort. In abstract interpretation, you kind of solving all paths at the same time, you are building a graph of possible jumps <@!273808422753796097> TeamX from Pegasys did a little shuffling AFAIK <@!636680106630316033> and <@!461762841641484302> are the two to ask -- I think the intuition is that things like static analysis and code chunking based on functionId aren't going to offer witness savings enough to make it worth the effort, but that fixed chunking (of variable or strictly enforced chunk sizes) might be worth it. But data will take a few more weeks to compile <vbuterin> Chunk based definitely seems like the natural way to Merkle the code... <vbuterin> Btw one idea I had is that in addition to the Merkle root we could also add in the Kate commitment of the code; this would allow O(1) sized witnesses (plus the code) for any subset of the code it would be cool to create the "machinery" (process) with which we can change the state merkelisation rules more often (more often than "never" at least, 🙂 )
